title: Poulet à la Moutarde
subtitle: Chicken in a Dijon mustard and cream sauce
excerpt: Chicken thighs braised in a sauce of Dijon mustard, white wine, and crème fraîche. The mustard mellows as it cooks, giving the sauce a gentle heat and depth without sharpness.
sourceNotes: Poulet à la moutarde is a classic of Burgundy and Dijon, the mustard capital of France. Elizabeth David documents it in French Provincial Cooking (1960). The Dijon mustard industry traces to the 14th century; the specific dish is a natural pairing of the region's two products, Dijon mustard and wine.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce can be made a day ahead without the crème fraîche. Add the crème fraîche and warm gently when reheating.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cultured cream with a slightly tangy flavour and a fat content high enough to prevent curdling when added to hot sauces. It is the standard enricher in French cream sauces, where double cream would split.

content.text: Poulet à la moutarde is chicken braised with Dijon mustard, white wine, and

. The mustard goes in both at the start (rubbed onto the raw chicken) and at the end (stirred into the finished sauce), which layers the flavour without making the dish harsh. The whole thing cooks in under 45 minutes, making it one of the faster French bistro dishes.
Rub the chicken thighs all over with 1 tsp of the Dijon mustard and season with salt and pepper.
Heat the oil and butter in a wide sauté pan over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken, skin-side down, for 5 minutes until golden. Turn and cook 3 minutes more. Remove and set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the shallots and cook for 4 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and thyme and cook for 1 minute more.
Pour in the wine, scraping up any browned bits. Simmer for 3 minutes until reduced by half.
Return the chicken to the pan, skin-side up. Cover and cook over low heat for 20 to 25 minutes until cooked through.

Remove the chicken. Stir the crème fraîche and remaining 2 tsp of mustard into the pan juices. Warm through over low heat for 2 minutes. Do not boil after adding the crème fraîche. Taste and season. Return the chicken to the pan and serve.

items.symptom: The sauce has split or curdled
items.cause: The crème fraîche was added to a pan that was too hot, or it was boiled after being added.
items.fix: Remove from the heat and whisk vigorously. The sauce should come back together. Next time, add the crème fraîche off the heat and warm it gently.

items.symptom: The mustard flavour is very sharp
items.cause: Too much mustard was added, or the second addition of mustard was stirred in over high heat.
items.fix: Add a little more crème fraîche to mellow the flavour. The heat-sensitive compounds in Dijon mustard become sharper if cooked at high temperature; always add the finishing mustard off the heat or on the lowest setting.

items.cause: The wine did not reduce enough before the chicken went back in.
items.fix: Remove the chicken and reduce the sauce on the hob, uncovered, for 2 to 3 minutes before adding the crème fraîche.

items.symptom: The chicken skin is not crisp
items.cause: The lid created steam that softened the skin.
items.fix: Remove the lid for the last 5 to 10 minutes of cooking. The sauce can reduce a little while the skin firms up.

content.text: Dijon has been the centre of French mustard production since at least the 14th century, when the city gained the right to regulate the trade. Chicken with Dijon mustard and cream is a dish from Burgundy. The region is known for its straightforward, well-made food, and this dish fits that tradition well. It has appeared on bistro menus across France for generations. Outside France it gained a following partly through the recipes of Elizabeth David, who described Burgundian cooking in her 1960 book French Provincial Cooking.
